title: Count Number of Teams
statement:
Soldiers stand in a row, and `rating[i]` is the rating of the soldier at position `i`; no two soldiers share a rating. A team is any three soldiers at positions `i < j < k` whose ratings either rise strictly (`rating[i] < rating[j] < rating[k]`) or fall strictly (`rating[i] > rating[j] > rating[k]`) from left to right.

Return how many different teams exist. One soldier may belong to any number of teams.
constraints: All values in rating are distinct
notes:
## Intuition

Trying every triple `i < j < k` is correct but costs O(n³), about 1.7·10^8 checks for 1000 soldiers. Enumerate only the middle soldier `j` instead. A rising team through `j` pairs any smaller rating on its left with any larger rating on its right, and those choices are independent, so their counts multiply. A falling team pairs a larger rating on the left with a smaller one on the right. Since all ratings differ, every other soldier is strictly smaller or strictly larger than `rating[j]`.

## Approach

1. For each middle position `j` from 1 to `n - 2`:
2. Scan the left side and count `leftLess` (smaller ratings) and `leftMore` (larger ratings).
3. Scan the right side and count `rightLess` and `rightMore` the same way.
4. Add `leftLess * rightMore` (rising teams) plus `leftMore * rightLess` (falling teams) to `teams`.
5. Return `teams`.

## Example 1, step by step

`rating = [2,5,3,4,1]`.

- `j = 1` (5): left has 1 smaller, 0 larger; right has 3 smaller, 0 larger. Adds 1·0 + 0·3 = 0.
- `j = 2` (3): left has 1 smaller (2), 1 larger (5); right has 1 smaller (1), 1 larger (4). Adds 1·1 + 1·1 = 2: teams (2,3,4) and (5,3,1).
- `j = 3` (4): left has 2 smaller, 1 larger; right has 1 smaller, 0 larger. Adds 2·0 + 1·1 = 1: team (5,4,1).

Total `teams = 3`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n²): each middle soldier scans the whole row once. (A Fenwick tree over ranks brings this to O(n log n), which is not needed for n ≤ 1000.)
- Space: O(1): only counters.

## Pitfalls

- Count both directions; the falling teams are easy to forget.
- Multiply the left and right counts; adding them counts pairs, not teams.
- The middle soldier can never be the first or last one, so `j` runs from 1 to `n - 2`.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `n` | number of soldiers |
| `teams` | teams counted so far |
| `j` | position of the middle soldier |
| `leftLess`, `leftMore` | soldiers left of `j` with a smaller or larger rating |
| `rightLess`, `rightMore` | soldiers right of `j` with a smaller or larger rating |

narration.6: Try every soldier that can stand in the middle of a team.
narration.9: Look at every soldier to the left of the middle one.
narration.10: Is this left soldier rated lower than the middle one?
narration.11: Yes: it could start a rising team.
narration.13: No: it is rated higher, so it could start a falling team.
narration.18: Look at every soldier to the right of the middle one.
narration.19: Is this right soldier rated lower than the middle one?
narration.20: Yes: it could end a falling team.
narration.22: No: it could end a rising team.
narration.26: Pair left and right choices: lower-left with higher-right rise, higher-left with lower-right fall.
narration.28: Every team has exactly one middle soldier, so this counts each team once.
